title: Set membership lookup time complexity
prompt_markdown: What is the average time complexity of checking membership (`x in my_set`) in a Python set containing $N$ elements?

content.explanation: Because Python sets are implemented as hash tables, checking membership computes the hash of x and inspects the bucket in O(1) average time.

title: Hashable types requirement
prompt_markdown: Which of the following objects CANNOT be added as an element to a Python `set`?
hints: Look for the mutable data type.

content.explanation: Set elements must be immutable and hashable. Lists are mutable and unhashable, so attempting to add a list raises a TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'.

title: Set intersection operator
prompt_markdown: Which Python operator computes the `intersection` of two sets `A` and `B`?
hints: Think of the bitwise AND symbol.

content.explanation: `A & B` computes the intersection (common elements). `A | B` is union, `A - B` is difference, and `A ^ B` is symmetric difference.

title: Predict execution of Longest Consecutive Sequence
prompt_markdown: Given input array `nums = [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]`, trace how the set-based algorithm determines which numbers initiate a sequence streak. List all numbers that pass the `x - 1 not in num_set` condition.
hints: Only numbers whose predecessor is NOT in the set start a streak.

rubric: Identifies that 100 passes because 99 is not in set (streak: [100], len=1)
Identifies that 200 passes because 199 is not in set (streak: [200], len=1)
Identifies that 1 passes because 0 is not in set (streak: [1, 2, 3, 4], len=4)
Explains why 2, 3, and 4 are skipped (their predecessors exist in set)
content.reference_answer:
Numbers initiating a streak (where `x - 1 not in num_set`):
1. `100`: `99` not in set -> explores [100] (length 1)
2. `200`: `199` not in set -> explores [200] (length 1)
3. `1`: `0` not in set -> explores [1, 2, 3, 4] (length 4)

Numbers skipped: `2`, `3`, and `4` are skipped because their predecessors (`1`, `2`, `3`) exist in the set. This check guarantees that every sequence is traversed only once, maintaining strict $O(N)$ runtime.

title: Diagnose and fix quadratic list membership lookup
hints: Convert corpus to a set before checking membership.

rubric: Explains that `q not in corpus` takes O(N) linear time on a list for each of the M queries
Converts corpus to a set in O(N) time upfront
Performs O(1) set lookups for all M queries, achieving O(M + N) total time
content.reference_answer:
Diagnosis: In Python, `q not in corpus` performs a linear search over `corpus` taking $O(N)$ time. Executing this inside a loop over $M$ queries results in $O(M \times N)$ quadratic runtime.

Optimal $O(M + N)$ Refactor:
```python
def check_all_present(corpus: list[int], queries: list[int]) -> bool:
    corpus_set = set(corpus)  # O(N) conversion
    for q in queries:         # M iterations
        if q not in corpus_set:  # O(1) average lookup
            return False
    return True
```
Converting `corpus` to `corpus_set` takes $O(N)$ time. Each query check takes $O(1)$ time, yielding $O(N + M)$ total time.

title: Explain hash table collisions and set worst-case complexity in interviews
prompt_markdown: In an interview, you state that set lookups are $O(1)$. The interviewer asks: 'Can a set lookup ever take $O(n)$ time, and what causes that to happen?' Explain hash collision mechanics and open addressing.
hints: Discuss hash collisions, bucket scanning, and adversarial input.

rubric: Explains that set lookup is O(1) on average, but worst-case time is O(n)
Explains hash collisions: two different keys hash to the same table slot or cluster
Explains open addressing resolution: Python probes through alternative slots in the array until the target or an empty slot is found
Concludes that if all n elements collide into the same probe sequence, finding an element requires scanning all n slots
content.reference_answer:
1. Worst-Case Runtime:
While set operations are $O(1)$ on average, the theoretical worst-case time complexity is $O(n)$.

2. Hash Collisions & Probe Chains:
- Python sets use an open-addressing hash table with perturbation probing.
- When an element is added, Python computes `slot = hash(key) & mask`. If that slot is already occupied by a different key (a hash collision), Python calculates a probe sequence to find the next available slot.
- During a lookup (`key in my_set`), Python visits slots along that probe sequence until it either finds the key or encounters an empty slot.

3. How $O(n)$ Worst-Case Occurs:
If an adversarial input is constructed where all $n$ elements produce hash codes that collide onto the exact same probe sequence, the hash table degrades into a linked list. Every membership check must probe through all $n$ occupied slots, degrading lookup time from $O(1)$ to $O(n)$.

Python mitigates this in production using SIPHASH (with a randomized salt per process) to prevent hash flooding attacks.
